body: APQ3 (average absolute difference of amplitude) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the average absolute difference of the per-cycle amplitude between consecutive glottal cycles in a voiced speech signal. For N consecutive glottal cycles with amplitudes A_i, the perturbation is computed as APQ3 = (1/(3N)) * Σ_i |A_{i+1} - A_i| / ((1/N) * Σ_i A_i), reported in percent or in dB (20*log10(std/mean)). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle amplitude measure (peak or RMS). Small APQ3 indicates amplitude stability (normal phonation); large APQ3 indicates amplitude instability (dysphonia). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by acoustic analysis software (Praat, laryngology toolkits) from pitch-synchronous amplitude tracks; it persists as a documented measurement in voice-disorder assessment. e.g.: Praat's shimmer analysis reporting the APQ3 value; the Kay Bolt Multi-Dimensional Voice Analysis software displaying APQ3 in its voice-quality report | not: shimmer (the general category of amplitude perturbation, not the specific APQ3 computation); jitter (a period perturbation parameter, not an amplitude perturbation) [formal: scintillatio quotiens media absoluta | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

For a frequency band defined by lower and upper bounds [f_low, f_high) and a spectral decomposition with N frequency bins indexed i=1..N, each with a complex amplitude A_i and frequency f_i where f_low <= f_i < f_high: the distribution is the ordered vector v = (|A_1|^2, |A_2|^2, ..., |A_N|^2), where |A_i|^2 is the energy of bin i. The parameters are the band bounds and the spectral decomposition method. The persistence mechanism is the explicit storage of the N-tuple of non-negative scalars ordered by bin index. [formal: the mathematical representation | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cepstral sequence is an ordered array of cepstral coefficients indexed by coefficient position, representing signal characteristics in the cepstral domain. Parameters: (1) number of coefficients N (typically 12-20 for speech), (2) coefficient type — filterbank-based MFCC, DFT-based, or DCT-based cepstral coefficients, (3) normalization method — mean-normalized, variance-normalized, or raw. The persistence mechanism maps (coefficient type, count, normalization) to a fixed-length vector c[1..N] where each element c[i] represents the i-th cepstral coefficient. [formal: cepstrum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Jitter (period perturbation) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the cycle-to-cycle variation of the fundamental period in a voiced speech signal. For N consecutive glottal cycles with periods P_i, the perturbation is computed as APQ1 = (1/(N-1)) * Σ_i |P_{i+1} - P_i| / ((1/N) * Σ_i P_i), or equivalently the standard deviation of the periods divided by their mean, reported in percent or in absolute units (milliseconds or seconds). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle period measure, (3) the perturbation variant (APQ1 — average absolute difference, JRR — ratio, JDP — absolute difference). Small jitter indicates period stability (normal phonation); large jitter indicates period instability (dysphonia). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by acoustic analysis software (Praat, laryngology toolkits) from pitch-synchronous period tracks; it persists as a documented measurement in voice-disorder assessment. [formal: titubatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Glottal contact is the physical contact between the vocal folds during the glottal cycle, comprising the closed phase (folds in contact) and the transition phases (closing and opening). It is the spatial/physical phenomenon of vocal-fold apposition that, when modulated by subglottal pressure, generates the periodic airflow excitation of phonation. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0, glottal contact is partitioned into the contact interval (folds touching) and the non-contact interval (glottis open). Its parameters include the contact quotient (from the electroglottogram envelope) and the open quotient (ratio of open-phase duration to the period). It persists as a standardized physiological construct in speech science and clinical laryngology, measured by electroglottography and videostroboscopy. [formal: contactus glottidis | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Amplitude perturbation is a class of voice-quality parameters that quantify the cycle-to-cycle variation in the amplitude (energy level) of voiced speech. The general measure computes the normalized difference between consecutive cycle amplitudes: given N consecutive glottal cycles with amplitudes A_i, perturbation = normalized deviation of |A_{i+1} - A_i| relative to the mean amplitude. Named variants include: APQ3 (average absolute difference quotient over 3-cycle windows) and the standard deviation variant (standard deviation of cycle amplitudes divided by their mean). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal, (2) the pitch-synchronous segmentation at cycle boundaries, (3) the specific perturbation variant formula. Reported in percent or decibels (20*log10(std/mean)). Persistence mechanism: maintained as a measurement class by the discipline of laryngology and speech science; implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Praat, laryngology suites), taught in voice-disorder curricula, and standardized in clinical practice. [formal: perturbatio amplitude | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A spectral moment is a quantitative descriptor obtained by weighting each frequency bin of a spectral energy distribution by a power of its center frequency and summing across all bins. The n-th spectral moment is mu_n = sum_i (f_i^n * E_i) where f_i is the center frequency of bin i and E_i is the spectral energy in that bin. The zeroth moment yields total spectral energy; the first moment yields the energy-weighted mean frequency; the second central moment yields variance; higher moments characterize asymmetry (skewness) and tail heaviness (kurtosis). The construct persists as a parameterized computational routine implementable in software or hardware, standardized across audio analysis toolkits and music information retrieval systems. [formal: spectral_moment | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A Kaiser window is a parameterized family of window functions defined by the zeroth-order modified Bessel function. Its formula is: w(n) = I₀(πβ√(1−((2n−(N−1))/(N))²)) / I₀(πβ) for 0 ≤ n ≤ N−1, where I₀ is the zeroth-order modified Bessel function of the first kind, N is the window length, and β is the shape parameter. The β parameter controls the tradeoff between main-lobe width and side-lobe attenuation: β = 0 yields a rectangular window; β = 2.43 is optimal for DFT analysis; β = 3.44 approximates a Hamming window; β = 5 gives ≈−43 dB side lobes; β = 6 gives ≈−47 dB; β ≥ 9 approaches the Blackman-Harris form. The family is designed to achieve the maximum main-lobe concentration for a given side-lobe level — optimal for a specified side-lobe constraint. Persistence mechanism: the Bessel-function formula codified in DSP literature and implemented in all major signal-processing toolkits. [formal: fenestra kaißer | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.5]

Spectral-band-smoothness is a spectral analysis measure that quantifies how smoothly the per-bin energy values change across frequency within a defined frequency sub-band of a spectrum. It computes a weighted mean absolute derivative of adjacent bin energies, normalized by the sub-band's mean energy and the number of bins, yielding a dimensionless index of spectral continuity. Parameters: the frequency sub-band bounds (f_min, f_max), the FFT bin energy vector, and optionally a window function for the energy estimation. The persistence mechanism is the algorithmic computation over the sub-band's energy profile. [formal: smoothness | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.30]

The maximum flow derivative (MFD) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the peak rate of change of glottal flow within a glottal cycle, reported per cycle and aggregated over voiced frames. Given the glottal flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, MFD is computed as the maximum magnitude of the first derivative (or first difference) of g within each pitch-synchronous cycle, max |g(n+1) - g(n)|, then aggregated across cycles by the median or mean over the analyzed frames. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) — the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the per-cycle window, (3) the derivative operator — first difference or finite difference over the sampled flow, (4) the normalization choice — absolute units (volume per sample interval) or relative to the cycle's maximum flow, and (5) the cross-cycle aggregation (median or mean). A high MFD marks a sharp glottal closure (pressed, spiky phonation) and a low MFD marks a gradual closure (breathy phonation), with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. It is reported in standardized units and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Praat, laryngology suites), documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained alongside jitter, shimmer, and the phase quotients. [formal: derivatio fluminis maxima | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

For a frequency band with N energy bins having energies E_1, E_2, ..., E_N: the RMS energy is the square root of the mean of squared energies. The parameter is the frequency band definition (lower and upper bounds). The persistence mechanism is RMS = sqrt((1/N) * sum(E_i^2)) over N bins within the band. Display trailer: [formal: rms energy | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The subglottal pressure (SGP) is a laryngeal voice-quality parameter quantifying the air pressure in the subglottal space (the trachea immediately below the vocal folds) during phonation. It is measured with a pressure transducer - typically a catheter placed through the nose or mouth, or an esophageal or transoral catheter - positioned below the glottis, and reported as the steady-state or cycle-averaged pressure during phonation, in units of cmH2O or kPa. A high SGP indicates increased laryngeal adduction effort (hyperfunctional phonation, spasmodic dysphonia, laryngeal muscle-tension dysphonia); a low SGP indicates glottal insufficiency (incomplete closure, breathy phonation). Parameters: (1) the analyzed phonation segment, (2) the transducer position below the glottis (nasotracheal, transoral, or esophageal catheter), (3) the pressure reference and averaging window. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical parameter measured by transducer catheter, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained as a member of the voice-quality measurement map. e.g.: subglottal pressure from an esophageal catheter transducer in a laryngeal muscle-tension dysphonia study; subglottal pressure from a nasotracheal catheter in a spasmodic-dysphonia protocol | not: glottal flow waveform; sound-pressure-level [formal: pressio subglottalis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

For a spectral decomposition with N frequency bins indexed i=1..N, each with center frequency f_i and complex amplitude A_i, the per-bin energy vector is the ordered tuple v = (|A_1|², |A_2|², …, |A_N|²) of non-negative scalars ordered by bin index, each entry being the energy of its bin. It is parameterized by the decomposition and a bin range [i_min, i_max] within 1..N: at the full range the vector covers all bins of the spectrum; at a range covering exactly the bins whose centers fall in a frequency band [f_low, f_high) it is the band-restricted vector. Persistence mechanism: explicit storage of the ordered tuple as the substrate operand that spectral descriptors read their per-bin energies, means, centroids, and maxima from directly, rather than from any scalar summary. [formal: vector energiae binarum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-onset detects the emergence of new frequency content by measuring the increase in spectral energy between consecutive time frames. Given consecutive power spectra P[k,t] and P[k,t-1], the spectral onset function O[t] = max(P[k,t] - P[k,t-1], 0) summed across frequency bins. Parameters: (1) the power spectrum P[k,t] as the input domain, (2) the frame rate and windowing scheme, (3) the frequency band of interest. The persistence mechanism is the frame-to-frame difference of the power spectrum, thresholded by a half-wave rectifier, which distinguishes onset frames from sustained or decaying content. [formal: spectralis initium | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-subband partitions the frequency axis into a contiguous range [f_lower, f_upper] within the overall spectrum. Given a sampling rate F_s and N frequency bins indexed by k = 0..N-1, a subband is defined by index range [k_1, k_2] where f_lower = k_1·F_s/N and f_upper = (k_2+1)·F_s/N. Parameters: (1) the spectral resolution (bin width F_s/N), (2) the frequency range [f_lower, f_upper] defining the subband, (3) the spectral representation (power spectrum, magnitude spectrum, or coefficients) over which the subband operates. The persistence mechanism is the contiguous index range [k_1, k_2] over the frequency axis, which enables independent processing of frequency content within the band. [formal: spectralis subbanda | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The glottal source spectrum is the per-frame power spectrum of the glottal flow waveform g(n) (the glottogram): the spectral representation of the estimated glottal source over each voiced frame. Given the frame-aligned glottal-flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source - the glottal source spectrum for a frame is the power spectrum of g over that frame, typically the squared magnitude of the frame's discrete Fourier transform |G(f)|^2 (or its Welch/averaged estimate), expressed in dB and reported across the source-relevant band (classically 100-4000 Hz). Its parameters are: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, the sole operand, (2) the per-frame spectral estimate (window, overlap, averaging method), and (3) the reporting band and units (dB, the source-relevant frequency range). The source spectrum is a maintained diagnostic representation in its own right: its overall shape - the balance of energy between low and high frequencies - characterizes the glottal source and is read clinically (a steeply falling source spectrum marks a breathy, energy-decaying source; a flatter or high-frequency-forward source spectrum a bright, pressed source), and it is the operand from which the source-domain voice-quality measures (the glottal source spectral tilt, the source harmonicity, the glottal-to-noise ratio) are computed. It is reported in standardized units and persists as a maintained source-domain representation in voice-analysis toolkits and laryngology, implemented alongside the glottogram and the source parameters. [formal: spectrum fontis glottis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

The glottal pulse is the periodic excitation of airflow generated by vocal fold vibration during voiced phonation. It is the source excitation that, when filtered by the vocal-tract transfer function, produces the speech signal. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, the glottal pulse is identified per pitch period as the airflow excursion whose onset coincides with the glottal opening and whose decay returns the flow to baseline. Parameters: (1) the vocal fold vibration cycle generating the airflow pulse, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the pulse shape parameters — rise time, duration, and amplitude of the airflow excursion. It persists as a standardized source-excitation construct in speech science, implemented in voice-analysis and synthesis toolkits, taught in speech production curricula, and used to model the glottal source in source-filter separation. [formal: pulsus glottidis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Speaking fundamental frequency is a human-made acoustic parameter of speech: the average fundamental frequency of the voice signal during connected speech, measured as the mean of the fundamental frequency values across a sample of continuous speech. It is computed from a recorded speech sample by extracting the fundamental frequency at each analysis frame and averaging the values. It persists as a standardized speech parameter because it is defined by a repeatable measurement procedure applied to a recorded speech sample. e.g.: the speaking fundamental frequency measured in a patient during a voice assessment; the speaking fundamental frequency used as a baseline in a voice disorder diagnostic report; the speaking fundamental frequency compared before and after voice therapy | not: jitter (cycle-to-cycle variation of the fundamental frequency, not its mean); pitch (the perceptual attribute of fundamental frequency, not the measured parameter itself) [formal: f0 | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The glottal closure instant (GCI) is a voice-quality parameter locating the point of glottal closure within each glottal cycle: the instant at which the glottal airflow returns to baseline and the closed phase begins. In the pinned sense it is estimated from the glottal flow waveform (glottogram) g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking: within each pitch-synchronous cycle, the GCI is the time point of the cycle's minimum glottal flow - the flow trough returning to baseline - equivalently the point where the first derivative of the flow crosses zero from negative to positive. It is reported per cycle as a time point and as the normalized GCI (nGCI), the difference between successive closure instants divided by the intervening fundamental period, a dimensionless ratio with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation: a prolonged nGCI marks increased glottal closure as in spastic or hyperfunctional dysphonia, a shortened nGCI a breathy, insufficiently closed source. Parameters: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the per-cycle window, (3) the closure operator - the flow-minimum location, the first-derivative zero crossing from negative to positive within the cycle, (4) the normalized reporting - nGCI as a dimensionless ratio, (5) the cross-cycle aggregation (median or mean over the analyzed frames). It is reported in standardized units and persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained alongside the closure quotient, the open quotient, the maximum flow derivative, and the return phase. [formal: instant clausurae glottidis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Voice range profile is a human-made graph that maps a speaker's voice across pitch and loudness: the range of fundamental frequencies a voice can produce at each loudness level, plotted as a region in the frequency-intensity plane. It is generated by recording a voice while the speaker phonates sustained vowels across a pitch and loudness sweep, measuring the fundamental frequency and sound pressure level at each point, and plotting the outermost boundary of the achievable region. It persists as a standardized clinical tool because it is defined by a repeatable recording and plotting procedure applied to a voice sample. e.g.: a voice range profile plotted for a patient with vocal fold paralysis during a voice assessment; a normative voice range profile used as a reference in a voice clinic; a voice range profile compared before and after voice therapy to track recovery | not: spectrogram (a time-frequency visual display of a voice signal, not a pitch-loudness boundary map); audiogram (a hearing threshold plot across frequency, not a voice production map) [formal: vocogram | substrate: behavior | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

Text-linguistics is a human-made discipline of linguistics — the study of the structure, coherence, and function of extended texts (discourses) as structured wholes that extend beyond the sentence level. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the unit of analysis is the text or discourse as an integrated semantic-pragmatic entity, governed by relations of cohesion (grammatical and lexical ties across clauses), coherence (understandable logical and semantic connections), and communicative purpose (the function the text serves in interaction); (2) the analytical tools include discourse structure analysis (narrative, argumentative, expository patterns), information structure (theme-rheme, given-new), referential continuity (pronoun chains, anaphora resolution), and textual genre conventions that organize texts for specific communicative situations. Text-linguistics persists as a discipline that produces descriptions of textual organization across languages, models of discourse interpretation, and applications in text technology, rhetoric, discourse analysis, and language pedagogy. Paradigmatic cases: Halliday and Hasan's cohesion analysis, van Dijk's discourse semantics, rhetorical structure theory. [formal: textus-linguistica | substrate: mind | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Spectral-median (median frequency) is the full-spectrum energy-quantile summary that reports the frequency f_med at which half of the total spectral energy lies below and half above. Parameters: (1) the per-bin energy vector E = {E_i} over the full analyzed spectrum [f0, f_max), (2) the energy-weighted cumulative distribution C(f) = (sum of E_i for bins at frequency <= f) / (sum of all E_i), (3) the target quantile q, which the median fixes at q = 0.5; the reported value is the smallest frequency f such that C(f) >= q. It is a member of the same quantile family as spectral-rolloff, which fixes q at the 85% energy level: the median is the 50% level of that family and does not depend on a chosen high-level contour. It reads the full per-bin energy vector and carries no [f_low, f_high) band bounds, so it is a full-side summary rather than a band-local one. Persists as a standard energy-quantile summary in audio analysis, computed on the per-bin energy vector in MIR toolkits and reported in sound-description documentation. [formal: mediana spectri | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-crossover is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying the median energy location of a full spectrum at a given analysis frame, unbounded by any sub-band: the frequency at which the cumulative energy reaches 50 percent of the spectrum's total energy. Parameters: (1) the full set of frequency bins i=1..N with center frequencies f_i, (2) the per-bin energy values E_i = |A_i|^2 over the whole spectrum, (3) the analysis frame window. Computed by ordering the bins in ascending frequency, accumulating the per-bin energies until the running total first reaches half of the total energy sum, and taking the center frequency of the bin at that crossing. The value is in hertz: a low crossover means most energy sits below the median frequency (dark spectrum), a high crossover means energy is pushed toward the upper bins (bright spectrum). It is the whole-spectrum counterpart of spectral-band-crossover, which restricts the same cumulative test to bins within [f_low, f_high). It differs from spectral-centroid (energy-weighted mean, sensitive to high-energy outliers) and from spectral-rolloff (the cumulative crossing at an arbitrary threshold such as 85 percent, measuring brightness rather than the median). Being the 50th percentile of the energy distribution, the crossover is robust to heavy-tailed energy. Persistence: the standardized mathematical definition of the full-spectrum energy median in spectral analysis, implemented in audio analysis toolkits and MIR feature pipelines. [formal: medium spectrale | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-concentration is a spectral analysis measure quantifying how much of a spectrum's total energy is concentrated in a single specified bin, normalized by the spectrum's total energy. Given a spectrum with N bins having energies E_1, E_2, ..., E_N, the concentration at bin j is C_j = E_j / Σ_i E_i. The value ranges from 0 (energy spread across all bins) to approaching 1 (nearly all energy in one bin). Parameters: (1) the spectral estimate (periodogram, Welch's method, or spectrogram slice), (2) the per-bin energy vector across all frequency bins, (3) the target bin index j. Persistence mechanism: standardized definition of normalized per-bin energy share, used in audio analysis, speech processing, and music information retrieval as a level-invariant spectral descriptor. [formal: concentratio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Closure quotient (CQ) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the fraction of the fundamental period during which the glottis is closed in voiced phonation. From the frame-aligned glottal-flow waveform g(n) (glottogram) and the fundamental period T0, the closed phase is the interval between the flow minimum (Fmin) and the next flow maximum (Fmax) - or between the zero crossings of the flow derivative bounding the closed phase - and CQ = closed phase / T0, so CQ = 1 - OQ for the same frame. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform estimated per voiced frame, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the closed-phase extraction method (Fmin-Fmax difference or flow-derivative zero crossings). It is reported as a dimensionless ratio; the maintained reference range for typical phonation sits near 0.3-0.5, and an elevated closure quotient indicates prolonged glottal closure as in breathy or dysphonic phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software (Praat, laryngology suites) from the glottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. [formal: quota clausurae | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Residual signal is the per-sample difference signal r(n) = x(n) - x_hat(n), where x(n) is the observed signal and x_hat(n) is the reconstructed signal produced by a model system. The residual-signal captures what the model fails to account for: in speech processing, it is the glottal excitation waveform after removing the vocal-tract filter; in system identification, it is the model-error waveform that reveals unmodeled dynamics or noise. Computed by: (1) obtaining the model (e.g., an all-pole linear-prediction filter), (2) filtering the input to produce the model output, (3) subtracting the model output from the observed signal. Parameters: (1) the observed signal x(n), (2) the model structure and parameters, (3) the subtraction method. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic implementation in DSP software (Praat, MATLAB, Kaldi), documentation in signal processing literature, and standardized use in model evaluation, speech analysis, and adaptive filtering. [formal: residualis-signalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The vocal-tract model is a human-made model of the vocal tract as an acoustic filter cavity in speech production, describing how the shape of the vocal tract resonates to shape the glottal source into speech sounds. Parameters: area function along tract length, formant frequencies and bandwidths, articulatory positions. Persistence mechanism: the model is formalized as acoustic tube theory, implemented in speech synthesis and analysis software, and taught in phonetics; it persists as a reusable filter component of the source-filter framework. [formal: vocal-tract | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.07]

The attack-time is a non-negative real-valued duration representing the time elapsed from the onset of a sound to the peak of its amplitude envelope. Parameters: (1) the amplitude envelope function of the sound, (2) the detected onset point (zero-crossing of the envelope derivative), (3) the peak point (global maximum of the envelope within the attack phase). The persistence mechanism identifies the onset as the first zero-crossing of the envelope's first derivative after silence, and the peak as the local maximum of the envelope following that onset, then computes the time difference. [formal: attack-time | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.03]

Spectral increase is a metric capturing the temporal rise of spectral energy between consecutive analysis frames. Computed as the difference between the current frame's total spectral energy and the preceding frame's energy, normalized by the preceding frame's energy. Positive values indicate energy growth; negative values indicate decay. [formal: augmentatio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Asymmetry coefficient is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the asymmetry of the glottal airflow pulse within each glottal cycle: the ratio of the rising phase duration to the falling phase duration of the first derivative of the glottal flow waveform. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, the glottal cycle is partitioned into the rising phase (where g'(n) is positive, from minimum to maximum) and the falling phase (where g'(n) is negative, from maximum to minimum); the asymmetry coefficient is rising-phase duration / falling-phase duration. A coefficient near 1 indicates a symmetric pulse (typical modal phonation), while deviation from 1 indicates asymmetric closure — a longer falling phase (coefficient < 1) marks abrupt closure in pressed phonation, and a longer rising phase (coefficient > 1) indicates gradual closure in breathy phonation. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform g(n) — the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking which frames the cycle, (3) the first derivative of g(n) to locate phase boundaries. It is reported as a dimensionless ratio; maintained reference ranges separate typical from disordered phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed from the glottogram by voice-analysis software (Praat, laryngology suites), documented in the Dewaele glottal-source parameter set, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and maintained alongside the maximum-flow-derivative, the glottal-flow-declination-rate, the phase quotients, and the other glottal source parameters as a member of the voice-quality measurement map. e.g.: the asymmetry coefficient reported in a laryngology study comparing pressed and breathy phonation types; the asymmetry coefficient computed from a glottal-flow waveform in a laryngeal dysphonia case; the asymmetry coefficient value of 0.85 measured in a pressed-phonation assessment | not: glottal-flow-declination-rate (the steepest negative slope, not a ratio); maximum-flow-derivative (the peak positive slope, not a ratio) [formal: coeficiens inaequalitatis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

spectral-band-peak(f_low, f_high) = max{E[i]} for all bins i where f_low <= f_center[i] < f_high. Parameters: f_low (Hz, lower band boundary), f_high (Hz, upper band boundary), sampling_rate (Hz, determines bin center frequencies), n_fft (int, FFT window size). Persistence: pointwise maximum of the power spectral density within the band. [formal: spectral-band-peak | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The energy-envelope is the per-frame time series of a signal's energy, a human-made representation derived from a discrete-time waveform by framing, windowing, and magnitude squaring. Parameters: (1) the analysis frame length (typically 20-40 ms), (2) the hop between successive frames, (3) the window function applied within each frame (e.g. Hamming, Hanning), and (4) the squaring convention - raw x^2(t), windowed |w(t) x(t)|^2, or the per-frame sum that projects to short-time-energy as its scalar value. Distinction: it is the energy series, not the per-frame scalar (short-time-energy) and not the per-sample Hilbert amplitude (amplitude-envelope); it is the operand on which temporal-centroid (first moment of the energy envelope) and onset-related energy readings operate. Persistence mechanism: standardized windowed computation across audio analysis and speech toolkits (librosa, Essentia, HTK, Praat), encoded in published feature-extraction pipelines. [formal: envelopium energiae | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The spectral-power-distribution is a non-negative real-valued function over a discrete frequency domain representing how signal power is distributed across frequency bins. Computation: take the magnitude spectrum |X[k]| of the input signal, compute P[k] = |X[k]|² / N for each bin k, yielding a discrete distribution over frequencies. Spectral-band-variance is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying the dispersion of spectral energy within a defined frequency sub-band of a spectrum at a given analysis frame. It is the band-localized (second-moment) statistic of the spectral-band moment family, computed from the per-bin energy values inside the band. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds (f_low, f_high, e.g. ISO 266 third-octave band edges or analyst-specified limits), (2) the per-bin energy array E_i = |X[k]|^2 indexed by the frequency bins whose centers fall within [f_low, f_high). Computation: the within-band mean mu = (1/N) SUM E_i, then the within-band variance sigma^2 = (1/N) SUM (E_i - mu)^2; the result is a single scalar per frame, typically in normalized relative units or joules squared. It measures how spread out the energy is across the band's bins: a concentrated band (one dominant bin) has low band-variance, an evenly spread band has high. Persistence: recomputed from the input spectrum and the band boundaries at any point in an audio analysis pipeline; it is the second-moment counterpart of spectral-band-centroid (first moment) and the even-order companion to spectral-band-skewness (third) and spectral-band-kurtosis (fourth). Jitter RAP (relative average perturbation) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the relative average of second-order cycle-to-cycle period differences, computed as the mean absolute value of the second difference of consecutive pitch periods divided by the mean pitch period, expressed in percent. For N consecutive glottal cycles with periods P_i, RAP equals the sum over i from 2 to N-1 of the absolute value of P_{i+1} minus 2 times P_i plus P_{i-1}, divided by N minus 2, all divided by the mean of all P_i. Parameters: the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, and the per-cycle fundamental period from pitch tracking. Small RAP indicates smooth, stable period progression (normal phonation); large RAP indicates erratic period changes (dysphonia). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by acoustic analysis software from pitch-synchronous period tracks; it persists as a documented measurement in voice-disorder assessment and clinical voice analysis reports. e.g.: The RAP jitter value displayed in the Kay Bolt MDVP jitter analysis report panel; RAP computed from sustained vowel phonation in the GRBAS voice assessment protocol using MDVP software; RAP reported in the acoustic analysis of dysphonia severity in the laryngology literature by Dewaele et al. | not: APQ1 using first-order average absolute difference; JRR the jitter ratio using simple cycle-to-cycle difference; shimmer using amplitude perturbation rather than period perturbation [formal: titubatio relativa | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

Spectral-band-evenness is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying how uniformly energy is distributed across the frequency bins within a defined frequency sub-band, normalized by the band's mean energy. It is the coefficient of variation of the per-bin energy values: given a band with N bins having energies E_i for i=1..N, the evenness is σ/μ where μ = (1/N)·ΣE_i is the mean energy and σ = √((1/N)·Σ(E_i - μ)²) is the standard deviation of energies. The value is a dimensionless ratio: 0 when all bins carry identical energy (perfectly even), increasing without upper bound as energy becomes more concentrated in fewer bins. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds (f_low, f_high), (2) the per-bin energy vector E_i within those bounds. Persistence mechanism: standardized definition of energy dispersion normalized by mean, used in music information retrieval and audio classification as a level-invariant spectral descriptor. Formant frequency is a human-made acoustic parameter of speech: a resonance frequency of the vocal tract that appears as a concentration of energy in the speech spectrum. Spectral-band-crossover is a spectral analysis parameter indicating the frequency within a defined sub-band at which the cumulative energy reaches 50% of the band's total energy — the band-local median frequency. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds, (2) the spectral energy values across frequency bins within the band. Computed by sorting frequency bins in ascending order by frequency, accumulating energy until the accumulated total reaches half the band's total energy; the frequency at that point is the crossover point. An analytic signal is a human-made complex-valued signal representation constructed from a real-valued signal x(t) by adding its Hilbert transform H{x(t)} as the imaginary component: z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}. This construction eliminates all negative-frequency components, resulting in a one-sided spectrum. The analytic signal carries three directly accessible parameters: (1) instantaneous amplitude (envelope) A(t) = |z(t)| = √(x(t)² + H{x(t)}²), (2) instantaneous phase φ(t) = arg(z(t)), and (3) instantaneous frequency f_inst(t) = (1/2π)·dφ/dt. These parameters are computable in real time from a single observation, without ensemble averaging. The construction is used in communications (quadrature modulation/demodulation, SSB generation), audio analysis (phase vocoder phase unwrapping), geophysics, and biomedical signal processing. Persistence mechanism: algorithmic computation standard in DSP libraries (scipy.signal.hilbert, MATLAB hilbert) and embedded in communication system designs. [formal: signalis analyticus | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-band-asymmetry is a statistical descriptor quantifying how unevenly spectral energy is distributed across the frequency bins within a defined sub-band. Parameters: (1) lower and upper frequency bounds of the sub-band, (2) the energy values per frequency bin within the band. Computed as the normalized sum of absolute deviations from the band centroid: A = sum_i(|f_i - f_c| * E_i) / sum_i(E_i), where f_i is the frequency of bin i, f_c is the band centroid (weighted mean frequency), and E_i is the energy in bin i. The value is expressed in Hertz and indicates the spatial spread of energy around the centroid — higher values mean energy is concentrated toward one edge of the band, lower values mean energy is more centrally distributed. Persistence mechanism: arithmetic computation over the finite set of per-bin energy values for the given band and analysis frame. [formal: asymmetria spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral peak position is the frequency bin index (or frequency in Hz) of the maximum spectral energy magnitude within a spectrum or subband. Used to identify dominant resonant components. Instantaneous frequency is a human-made signal processing construct that measures the rate of change of the phase of a signal at each moment in time. It is defined as: f_inst(t) = (1/2π)·dφ(t)/dt, where φ(t) = arg(z(t)) is the instantaneous phase of the analytic signal z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}, constructed from a real-valued signal x(t) and its Hilbert transform H{x(t)}. Unlike Fourier frequency (which represents a global property of the signal), instantaneous frequency is a local, time-varying quantity that tracks frequency modulation, chirp signals, and time-varying spectral content in real time. Parameters: (1) the phase unwrapping method applied to φ(t) (to avoid discontinuities at ±π), (2) the noise regularization method (to prevent divergence where amplitude is near zero). Persistence mechanism: standard in radar (chirp signal analysis), seismology, speech processing (formant tracking), and biomedical engineering (EEG/ECG frequency modulation analysis), implemented in DSP libraries and embedded in signal analysis instruments. [formal: frequency instantanea | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Shimmer (amplitude perturbation) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the cycle-to-cycle variation of amplitude in a voiced speech signal. Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle amplitude measure (peak or RMS), (3) the perturbation variant (APQ3 quotient or standard deviation). Small shimmer indicates amplitude stability (normal phonation); large shimmer indicates amplitude instability (dysphonia). It is computed from the glottal-flow waveform g(t) and the glottal-cycle period T0: the closed phase runs from glottal-pulse onset to the instant the flow returns to baseline, and the quotient is the closed-phase duration divided by T0. The Hilbert transform is a linear operator that shifts the phase of every frequency component of a real-valued signal by 90 degrees (π/2 radians). Mathematically, for a signal x(t), the Hilbert transform is: H{x(t)} = (1/π) PV ∫₋∞^∞ x(τ)/(t−τ) dτ, where PV denotes the Cauchy principal value. In the frequency domain, it acts as an all-pass filter with frequency response H(f) = −j·sgn(f), multiplying positive frequencies by −j and negative frequencies by +j. The transform produces the quadrature component of x(t); combining x(t) with its Hilbert transform yields the analytic signal z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}, from which instantaneous amplitude (envelope), instantaneous phase, and instantaneous frequency can be derived. Parameters: (1) the input signal domain (continuous-time or discrete via DFT-based implementation), (2) handling of the zero-frequency component (typically set to 0). Persistence mechanism: implemented in DSP libraries (scipy.signal.hilbert, MATLAB hilbert), used in communications (SSB modulation/demodulation), geophysics, and vibration analysis. [formal: transform Hilbert | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

source-filter-separation is a human-made signal processing technique that decomposes an observed signal into two additive or convolutive components: a source (excitation) component representing the energy origin, and a filter (resonance) component representing the shaping mechanism. Parameters: (1) the input signal x(n), (2) the source-filter model assumptions (convolutive vs additive), (3) the decomposition method and its parameters. The glottal inertia quotient (GIQ) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the shape of the glottal area cycle: the ratio of the first to the zeroth moment of the glottal area waveform A(t) within each glottal cycle, GIQ = I1 / I0, where I_k = the integral of (t/T0)^k * A(t) dt over the cycle window T0. The electroglottogram is the demodulated envelope of the electroglottographic (EGG) voltage waveform. EGG passes a small alternating current through the vocal folds and records the voltage across them; because glottal contact area modulates vocal-fold impedance — high impedance when the glottis is open, low impedance when the folds are in contact — the peak-to-peak voltage amplitude is inversely proportional to glottal contact area. Demodulating the per-cycle peak-to-peak voltage produces a continuous time series whose amplitude is inversely proportional to glottal contact area, tracking the open/close cycle of the glottis. Parameters: (1) the excitation current — a small AC current kept below the safety threshold (typically ~0.5 mA peak at ~2.5 kHz); (2) electrode placement — two submental/neck electrodes completing the current path through the larynx; (3) demodulation — per-cycle peak-to-peak voltage measurement producing a continuous signal. The electroglottogram persists as a measured time series of glottal contact in clinical laryngology and voice-disorder assessment (e.g., Kay PENTAGRAM, the laryngograph). [formal: electroglottogramma | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Creaky voice (vocal fry) is a classification category for a mode of voiced phonation defined by a specific glottal configuration: the vocal folds are adducted with loose medial contact and low subglottal pressure, vibrating at a low fundamental frequency (typically well below the modal range) in an aperiodic, implosive cycle in which glottal flow falls to zero and briefly reverses near cycle end, producing a sawtooth-like flow waveform and the audible creak or fry sound. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal configuration — medial adduction with loose contact and reduced subglottal pressure, (2) the cycle signature — low f0, aperiodic implosive cycles with flow reversal, (3) the acoustic signature — a low, creaky, grainy timbre with a sparse, weakly harmonic structure. It persists as a named mode of the phonation-mode taxonomy: documented in laryngology and phonetics, used in voice-disorder assessment (creaky voice as a compensatory or pathological voice quality) and in voice training (vocal fry contrasted with modal voice), and maintained alongside the other voice modes. e.g.: the vocal fry mode at the ends of utterances in casual American English, labeled in phonetic transcription; the vocal fry category in Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory; the creaky voice quality labeled in a laryngology report for a patient with a strained low-pitched voice | not: breathy voice (incomplete closure with modal-frequency vibration and turbulent noise leakage); modal phonation (the normal periodic mode, a different mode of the same taxonomy); whisper voice (unvoiced glottal airflow, outside voiced phonation) [formal: vox crepitans | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

Contact quotient (Cn) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the fraction of the fundamental period T0 during which the vocal folds are in contact in voiced phonation. From the electroglottographic signal (EGG) or glottal-flow waveform g(n), the contact phase is the interval during which the signal indicates vocal fold contact, and Cn = contact phase / T0. Parameters: (1) the electroglottographic or glottal-flow signal estimated per voiced frame, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the contact-phase extraction method (EGG derivative zero crossings or glottal-flow extrema). It is reported as a dimensionless ratio; the maintained reference range for typical phonation sits near 0.5-0.7, and an elevated contact quotient indicates prolonged vocal fold contact as in pressed or hypofunctional phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software (Praat, laryngology suites) from the glottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. The skewness (third standardized moment) of a power spectrum around its spectral centroid. Parameters: (1) a frequency-binned power or magnitude spectrum S[k] for k=0..K-1, (2) the spectral centroid μ = Σ_k f[k]·S[k] / Σ_k S[k], (3) the spectral bandwidth σ = sqrt(Σ_k (f[k]-μ)²·S[k] / Σ_k S[k]). Computation: skewness = Σ_k (f[k]-μ)³·S[k] / (σ³·Σ_k S[k]). Persistence: the scalar value is stored per spectral frame and recomputed when the spectrum changes. Positive skewness indicates a spectrum with a long tail toward higher frequencies; negative skewness indicates a tail toward lower frequencies.

Spectral-evenness is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying how uniformly energy is distributed across the frequency bins of a full spectrum at a given analysis frame, unbounded by any sub-band: the coefficient of variation of the per-bin energies. Parameters: (1) the full set of frequency bins i=1..N, (2) the per-bin energy values E_i = |A_i|^2 over the whole spectrum, (3) the analysis frame window. Computed as evenness = sigma/mu, where mu = (1/N) SUM E_i is the arithmetic mean of the per-bin energies and sigma = sqrt((1/N) SUM (E_i - mu)^2) is their standard deviation. The value is a dimensionless ratio: 0 when every bin carries identical energy (a perfectly flat spectrum), increasing without upper bound as energy concentrates in fewer bins. Being a ratio of two homogeneous quantities, it is level-invariant: scaling all bin energies by a constant leaves it unchanged. It is the whole-spectrum counterpart of spectral-band-evenness, which computes the same ratio over bins within [f_low, f_high). It differs from spectral-entropy (Shannon information content of the normalized energy distribution, bounded, logarithmic scale) and from spectral-flatness (geometric-mean-to-arithmetic-mean ratio, measuring flatness on a multiplicative scale): evenness is the dispersion of energies normalized by the arithmetic mean on an additive scale. Persistence: the standardized mathematical definition of full-spectrum energy uniformity in spectral analysis, implemented in audio analysis toolkits and MIR feature pipelines. [formal: aequabilitas spectrale | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Effective bandwidth is a scalar width descriptor of a signal's spectral (or line) energy distribution, defined as the width of the ideal rectangular pulse having the same peak height and the same total energy as the distribution. Parameters: (1) the per-bin energy values E_i (i = 1..N) of the spectral representation; (2) the per-bin frequency spacing delta_f. Computed as BW_eff = (sum(E_i) / max_i E_i) * delta_f: the dimensionless ratio of total energy to peak energy, scaled to frequency units (Hz). Unlike the centroid-spread bandwidth (the second central moment), it contains no centroid term: for a single-bin (pure-tone) distribution it yields delta_f, the width of one bin, and for a flat distribution over N bins it yields N * delta_f, the full occupied support. Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle fundamental period measure. Its parameters are: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle fundamental period measure from pitch tracking, (3) the cross-cycle aggregation (standard deviation over mean period). The glottal flow declination rate (GFD) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the steepest negative slope of the glottal airflow pulse within each glottal cycle: the maximum magnitude of the falling (negative) portion of the first derivative of the glottal flow, a measure of how abruptly the vocal folds close. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, the sole operand, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the per-cycle window, (3) the derivative operator - first difference or finite difference over the sampled flow, (4) the directional selection - the negative (declination) branch of the derivative only, (5) the cross-cycle aggregation (median or mean). A high GFD marks an abrupt glottal closure (pressed, spiky phonation); a low GFD marks a gradual, incomplete closure (breathy, hyperfunctional phonation), with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. It is reported in standardized units and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology (the Dewaele glottal-source parameter set), and maintained alongside the maximum flow derivative, the glottal closure instant, the phase quotients, jitter, and shimmer. e.g.: GFD reported per frame in a laryngeal muscle-tension dysphonia study; GFD of a creaky-voice glottogram in a voice-disorder case report; GFD computed from an EGG-based glottogram in a pressed-phonation assessment | not: maximum flow derivative MFD (max magnitude of g' in both directions); return phase (a duration, not a slope) [formal: declivitas fluminis glottidis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

The persistence mechanism is the algorithmic computation over the band energy vector per analysis frame, persisting as a time series of dimensionless scalars. The glottal source spectral tilt (GSS) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the slope of the glottal source spectrum: the linear-regression slope of the log power spectrum of the glottal flow waveform g(n) versus log frequency, reported in dB/octave. From the frame-aligned glottal-flow waveform g(n) (glottogram), the per-frame power spectrum of g is estimated, the log-log regression of log PSD against log frequency is fitted over the regression band (classically 100-4000 Hz), and the slope is the source spectral tilt for that frame; frames are aggregated by median or mean over the analyzed voiced frames. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, the sole operand, (2) the per-frame power-spectrum estimate of g (window, smoothing), (3) the regression band (classically 100-4000 Hz), (4) the regression method - log-log linear fit of the source PSD, and (5) the cross-frame aggregation (median or mean). A cepstrum is the power spectrum of the log-power spectrum of a signal. Computed by: taking the Fourier transform of the signal, computing the log of the magnitude spectrum, then computing the inverse Fourier transform of the log-magnitude spectrum. Parameters: window size for the initial transform, overlap for overlap-add reconstruction. The cepstrum separates periodic structures in the spectrum (such as formant echoes in speech or pitch harmonics) into distinct peaks at quefrency positions corresponding to the delay between reflections. Persistence mechanism: the cepstrum is computed as a deterministic mathematical transform, implemented in speech analysis and audio processing software, and used as an intermediate representation in cepstral feature extraction pipelines. Spectral-par is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying the contrast between the strongest and the average spectral energy across the frequency bins of a full spectrum at a given analysis frame, unbounded by any sub-band. It is the ratio of the maximum per-bin energy to the arithmetic mean of the per-bin energies: PAR = max_i(E_i) / ( sum_i E_i / N ), where E_i = |X[k_i]|^2 is the per-bin energy over the whole spectrum for frequency bins i=1..N. Parameters: (1) the full set of frequency bins i=1..N with their per-bin energies, (2) the analysis frame window. The value is dimensionless: a large PAR means energy is concentrated in a few dominant peaks, a small PAR means a flat spectrum. It is the whole-spectrum counterpart of spectral-band-peak-to-average-ratio, which restricts the same ratio to bins within [f_low, f_high). Persistence: the standardized mathematical definition of full-spectrum peak contrast in spectral analysis, implemented in audio analysis toolkits (e.g. the par feature of librosa) and MIR feature pipelines. critical-band is a psychoacoustic CONCEPT describing the frequency resolution limits of the auditory system: a bandpass region within which the ear integrates acoustic energy as a single unit. The canonical parameterization is the Bark scale, mapping frequency (Hz) to critical-band number (0-24), where each band corresponds approximately to the bandwidth of a single auditory-filter channel at that frequency. The concept is mathematically approximated by the ERB rate function ERB(f) = 24.7*(4.37*f + 1) where f is in kHz, and by Zwicker-frequency (Bark) scale values. Open quotient (OQ) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the fraction of the fundamental period during which the glottis is open in voiced phonation. From the frame-aligned glottal-flow waveform g(n) (glottogram) and the fundamental period T0, the open phase is the interval between the flow maximum (Fmax) and the flow minimum (Fmin) — or between the zero crossings of the flow derivative — and OQ = open phase / T0. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform estimated per voiced frame, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the open-phase extraction method (Fmax–Fmin difference or flow-derivative zero crossings). It is reported as a dimensionless ratio; the maintained reference range for typical phonation sits near 0.5–0.7, and a reduced open quotient indicates excessive glottal closure. Electroglottography (EGG) is a non-invasive technique that measures glottal vocal-fold contact over time by passing a small alternating current through the vocal folds and recording the voltage across them. Because the glottal contact area modulates the electrical impedance of the vocal folds — high impedance when the glottis is open (air gap), low impedance when the folds are in contact — the peak-to-peak amplitude of the voltage is inversely related to glottal contact area, and its demodulated envelope, the electroglottogram (EGG waveform), tracks the open/close cycle of the glottis. Parameters: (1) excitation current — a small AC current kept below the safety threshold (typically ~0.5 mA peak at ~2.5 kHz); (2) electrode placement — two submental/neck electrodes completing the current path through the larynx; (3) demodulation — per-cycle peak-to-peak voltage measurement producing a continuous signal; (4) output — the electroglottogram, a time series whose amplitude is inversely proportional to glottal contact area. Persistence mechanism: standardized EGG transducers and laryngeal analysis systems (Kay PENTAGRAM, the laryngograph), documented in clinical laryngology and voice-disorder assessment; the waveform persists as a measured time series of glottal contact. [formal: electroglottographia | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

An equivalent-rectangular-bandwidth (ERB) is a human-made, frequency-dependent unit of filter bandwidth used to describe the frequency selectivity of the auditory periphery. It is defined as the width of a rectangular (flat) bandpass filter that would pass the same energy as a given auditory filter centered at frequency f. The standard empirical expression is ERB(f) = 24.7·(4.37·f + 1), with f in kHz and the result in Hz, so the equivalent width is about 104 Hz near 0.1 kHz and grows toward roughly 100·f at high frequencies — the auditory filter narrows relative to its center as f rises. Parameters: (1) the center frequency f (kHz); (2) the chosen fitting curve — the Glasberg & Moore (1990) expression is canonical, with alternative fits in the literature. Persistence mechanism: it persists as a standard psychophysically derived formula carried in the audiology and auditory-modeling literature (Glasberg & Moore 1990; Moore's auditory-filter and loudness work) and applied operationally to set the spacing and bandwidth of gammatone, bark, and auditory-filter-bank filters. Boundary: it is a unit of measure — a single number in Hz attached to a center frequency — not the auditory filter itself, not a signal's spectral bandwidth, and distinct from the generic signal-processing 'bandwidth' entry. [formal: latitudo rectanguli aequivalens | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-band-spread is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying the dispersion of spectral energy across the frequency bins within a defined frequency sub-band of a spectrum at a given analysis frame. It is the square root of the band's second central moment: the energy-weighted standard deviation of bin frequencies about the band's centroid. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds (f_low, f_high), (2) the per-bin energy values E_i = |X[k]|^2 for bins whose center frequencies fall within [f_low, f_high), (3) the analysis frame window. Computed as spread = sqrt( sum E_i * (f_i - c)^2 / sum E_i ), where c = sum(f_i * E_i) / sum(E_i) is the spectral-band-centroid of the same band. The value is in hertz: a large spread means energy is dispersed across the band, a small spread means energy is concentrated near the centroid. Persistence: the standardized mathematical definition of band dispersion in spectral analysis, implemented in audio analysis toolkits (e.g. librosa's spectral_spread) and MIR feature pipelines. Computation: sort P[k] by f[k], compute cumulative sum C[k] = Σ_{i=0}^{k} P[i], then find the smallest k* such that C[k*]/Σ_{i=0}^{N-1} P[i] ≥ τ; roll-off = f[k*]. spectral-band-mode is a CONCEPT filing for a spectral analysis parameter that identifies the mode of the spectral energy distribution within a defined frequency sub-band. Persistence mechanism: the frequency bin with the highest spectral energy amplitude within the defined sub-band, computed as argmax of the band-limited energy histogram. The mode indicates the dominant spectral component within a narrow sub-band, complementing the centroid (mean) and variance (spread) descriptors. [formal: spectral-band-mode | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A critical-band is a human-made psychoacoustic construct representing the frequency resolution unit of the human auditory system — the effective bandwidth of auditory filters at a given center frequency. It quantifies how the ear's basilar membrane separates frequencies into perceptually independent channels. At any center frequency f, the critical-band width approximates the ERB(f) = 24.7·(4.37·f+1) Hz (f in kHz), which is the width of a rectangular bandpass filter passing the same energy as the auditory filter at that frequency. Parameters: (1) center frequency f; (2) the bandwidth rule (ERB approximation). Persistence mechanism: it persists as a standard psychoacoustic concept codified in Zwicker's work (Zwicker 1961, 'Schnell und zeitliche Abhängigkeit der Lautheit'), ITU-R BS.516, ISO 532, and carried in audio analysis, sound design, and psychoacoustic modeling literature. Boundary: it is a model of perceptual frequency resolution, not the physical basilar membrane itself, not the gammatone filter realization, and not the bark-scale (which maps frequencies onto critical-band numbers). [formal: banda critica | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral sparseness is a metric quantifying how concentrated spectral energy is across frequency bins. High sparseness indicates energy concentrated in few bins (e.g. tonal signals); low sparseness indicates diffuse energy (e.g. noise). Computed as (sum of magnitudes)^2 divided by (number_of_bins times sum of squared magnitudes). [formal: sparsitas spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An auditory-filter is a human-made linear bandpass filter whose center frequency and bandwidth are chosen to match the frequency selectivity of the auditory periphery at that frequency, so that it approximates the response of a single cochlear channel. The standard parameterization sets the bandwidth to the equivalent-rectangular-bandwidth ERB(f)=24.7·(4.37·f+1) at center f (kHz), with the filter shape given by a gamma-shaped (exponentially-modulated sinusoid) or Lorentzian (ROEX) impulse response. Parameters: (1) center frequency f; (2) the selectivity/bandwidth rule (ERB, or a constant-Q Lorentzian); (3) the impulse-response shape — the gamma (gammatone) form or the rectangular-excitation (ROEX/Lorentzian) form; (4) the cascade order when realized as resonator sections. Persistence mechanism: it persists as a standard model of single-channel cochlear selectivity in the auditory-periphery literature (the gammatone and ROEX families; Moore's and Glasberg & Moore's auditory-filter work) and is the element from which filter banks are built. Boundary: it is a single analysis filter, not the array (filter-bank / mel-filterbank) that places many in parallel, and not the gammatone-filter alone — the gammatone-filter is the canonical resonator realization of this construct, so the two are distinct kinds, not the same thing. [formal: filtrum auditivum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-spread is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying the dispersion of spectral energy across the frequency bins of a full spectrum at a given analysis frame, unbounded by any sub-band. It is the square root of the spectrum's second central moment: the energy-weighted standard deviation of bin frequencies about the full-spectrum centroid. Parameters: (1) the full set of frequency bins i=1..N with center frequencies f_i, (2) the per-bin energy values E_i = |X[k_i]|^2 over the whole spectrum, (3) the analysis frame window. Computed as spread = sqrt( sum_i E_i * (f_i - c)^2 / sum_i E_i ), where c = sum_i(f_i * E_i) / sum_i(E_i) is the full-spectrum spectral-centroid. The value is in hertz: a large spread means energy is dispersed across the spectrum, a small spread means energy is concentrated near the centroid. It is the whole-spectrum counterpart of spectral-band-spread, which restricts the same formula to bins within [f_low, f_high). Persistence: the standardized mathematical definition of full-spectrum dispersion in spectral analysis, implemented in audio analysis toolkits and MIR feature pipelines. [formal: dispersio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Phonation is the process of producing sound by the vibration of the vocal folds during voiced phonation. It is the fundamental vocal mechanism that converts airflow from the lungs into an audible periodic signal. Given the subglottal air pressure P(t) and the vocal-fold contact area A(t), the phonation process generates the glottal flow waveform g(t) whose periodic excitation is filtered by the vocal tract to produce speech. Parameters: (1) subglottal air pressure generated by respiratory muscles, (2) vocal-fold contact area modulated by laryngeal muscle tension, (3) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking. It persists as a standardized physiological construct in speech science and clinical laryngology, implemented in voice-analysis toolkits and taught in speech production curricula. [formal: phonatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

The spectral-band-complexity is a CONCEPT that quantifies the number of independently varying components needed to describe the spectral shape of a frequency band. Parameters: a discrete spectral power distribution {P_i} over N frequency bins. Computed as the ratio of the effective number of bins (exp(H) where H = -Σp_i·log(p_i) is the Shannon entropy of the normalized distribution p_i = P_i/ΣP_j) to the actual number of bins N, yielding a dimensionless measure in (0,1] where 1 indicates maximal complexity (flat spectrum). Persistence: the scalar value is maintained for a given spectral band as long as the underlying spectral representation is stable. [formal: latin | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Modal phonation is the normal periodic mode of the phonation mode taxonomy: the mode in which the vocal folds vibrate with complete glottal closure each cycle, at a stable fundamental frequency within the speaker's modal range, producing periodic excitation of the vocal tract. It is the reference mode of the taxonomy: breathy and creaky phonation are defined against it, as deviations in closure and cycle character. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal configuration - medial adduction with complete closure each cycle (a high closure quotient) and firm contact, (2) the cycle signature - a stable f0 in the modal range with periodic, non-implosive cycles and no flow reversal, (3) the acoustic signature - a clean periodic tone with a strong harmonic series and minimal aperiodic noise. It persists as the reference mode of the phonation mode taxonomy: named in laryngology and phonetics, used in voice assessment (a breathy or creaky quality is classified as a deviation from modal) and in voice training (restoring or maintaining the modal mode), and maintained alongside the other modes in Sundberg's phonation inventory. e.g.: the modal-phonation mode in Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory; the 'modal voice' category on a voice therapy plan for a patient with habitual breathy voice; the 'modal voice' label in a phonetic description of a speaker's neutral sustained /a/ | not: breathy voice (incomplete closure with turbulent noise leak); creaky voice (low-f0 aperiodic implosive cycles); whisper (unvoiced glottal airflow) [formal: vox modalis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

A bark-spectrogram is a two-dimensional time-frequency matrix where rows are bark-scale frequency bins and columns are temporal frames. Parameters: (1) N bark-scale bins indexed 0..N-1, (2) frame hop size h in samples, (3) window function w applied per frame. Computation: for each frame f, apply FFT to windowed segment, convert linear-frequency indices to bark scale via Bark(f) = 13*arctan(0.00076*f) + 3.5*arctan((f/7500)^2), accumulate energy into bark bins, normalize by bin bandwidth. Persistence: the matrix values are the squared magnitudes accumulated per bark bin, stored as a sequence of N×T matrices. Display: a heatmap with time on the x-axis, Bark units on the y-axis, color representing log-energy.

Lexeme is a human-made conceptual category — the minimal meaningful unit of a language that functions as the basic item in the mental lexicon of speakers. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) minimal meaningfulness: the lexeme carries semantic content that cannot be decomposed into smaller meaningful parts within that language's grammar, distinguishing it from phrases or complex words whose meaning is compositional; (2) identity-independence: the lexeme has a single abstract identity across all its surface forms — inflectional variants (walk/walks/walked/walking) and allomorphic variants (happy/happiness) express the same lexeme, while a shift in core meaning or derivational structure marks a different lexeme; (3) mental reality: lexemes are stored and retrieved by speakers as discrete units in the mental lexicon, not as lists of word forms. Lexemes persist as the atomic referent of grammatical description, lexical semantics, and word-formation rules. [formal: lexema | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The parameter is the frequency band definition (lower and upper bounds). The persistence mechanism is the dimensionless ratio CF = max(E_i) * sqrt(N) / sqrt(sum(E_i^2)).
