Inverse-filtering is a signal processing technique that estimates and removes the effect of a known or estimated system transfer function from a signal, effectively recovering the original input that passed through that system. The method operates by: (1) obtaining the estimated transfer function H(z) of the system to be inverted (e.g., the linear-prediction filter for the vocal tract), (2) constructing the inverse filter H_inv(z) = 1/H(z), (3) filtering the observed signal with H_inv(z) to produce the residual or excitation signal. Parameters: (1) the transfer function to invert — typically a finite-order all-pole model estimated from the signal itself, (2) the input signal — the observed output of the system, (3) the inversion method — direct division in the z-domain, iterative regularization, or frequency-domain division. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic implementation: the inverse filter is encoded in DSP software (e.g., Praat, MATLAB, Kaldi), documented in signal processing textbooks, and standardized in speech analysis toolkits for source-filter separation. [formal: filtrum inversum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Formant dispersion (D) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the mean spacing between the first three formant frequencies of a voiced segment, reported in hertz as D = (F3 - F1) / 2, equivalently the mean of (F2 - F1) and (F3 - F2). Given formant estimates F1, F2, F3 per analysis frame, D is computed per frame from the frame's three lowest formant frequencies and aggregated across the voiced segment by mean (and, where maintained, standard deviation). Its parameters are: (1) the formant frequency estimates F1, F2, F3 per analysis frame — the vocal-tract resonances located by formant tracking, (2) the dispersion operator — (F3 - F1)/2 or the mean of consecutive spacings, (3) the cross-frame aggregation (mean, standard deviation, or median) over the analyzed voiced segment. A larger dispersion indicates a shorter, stiffer vocal tract (child-like or laryngectomized voice) and a smaller dispersion a longer tract, with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. It is reported in hertz and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained alongside jitter, shimmer, the phase quotients, and the noise ratios. [formal: diffusio formantorum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Voice tremor is a human-made measure of the amplitude modulation of phonation: the cycle-to-cycle variation in the fundamental frequency and intensity of the voice signal produced by the vocal folds. It is computed from a recorded voice signal by tracking the fundamental frequency across successive glottal cycles and measuring the amplitude of each cycle; the tremor rate is the number of modulation cycles per second and the tremor amplitude is the peak-to-peak variation expressed as a percentage of the mean amplitude. It persists as a standardized parameter in clinical voice assessment because it is defined by a repeatable measurement procedure applied to a recorded voice sample. e.g.: voice tremor measured in a patient with spasmodic dysphonia during a clinical voice assessment; tremor amplitude reported as a percentage in a voice disorder diagnostic report; a voice tremor standard used by a speech-language pathologist to quantify shaky voice | not: jitter (frequency modulation of the fundamental frequency); shimmer (intensity modulation of the voice signal) [formal: tremor | substrate: behavior | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

Spectral-crest is a dimensionless ratio expressing the concentration of spectral energy at the peak bin relative to the mean across all bins. Parameters: (1) a power spectrum P[k] or magnitude spectrum |X[k]| for k = 0, ..., N-1. When using power spectrum: crest = max(P[k]) / (1/N Σ P[k]). When using magnitude: crest = max(|X[k]|) / (1/N Σ |X[k]|). The ratio is expressed in dB: crest_dB = 10·log₁₀(crest). Display: crest = max_k(P[k]) / mean_k(P[k]) [formal: mind | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Voice onset time (VOT) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the temporal offset between the onset of the glottal source and the onset of acoustic voice in the first phonation cycle, typically measured after a voiceless context such as a plosive. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the acoustic waveform x(n), VOT is computed as the interval from the first flow maximum (first glottal closure, the glottal-source onset) to the first reliable periodic component of the acoustic signal (acoustic voice onset), reported in milliseconds. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform estimated per voiced frame (the glottogram), (2) the acoustic waveform with the first phonation cycle, (3) the onset-detection criterion for each endpoint (first flow maximum from the glottogram; periodicity onset by autocorrelation or waveform marking). It is reported in milliseconds; the maintained reference ranges separate phonation types — long (positive) VOT when acoustic onset leads glottal closure, breathy phonation; near-zero (short) VOT when the two onsets are simultaneous, modal phonation; negative VOT when glottal closure precedes acoustic onset, creaky phonation — and deviations mark glottal-source abnormalities. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software from the glottogram and acoustic waveform, taught in voice-disorder curricula and speech-language pathology, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. [formal: tempus initii vocis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Spectral-band-rolloff is a spectral analysis parameter indicating the frequency below which a specified percentage (typically 85%) of the total spectral energy within a defined frequency sub-band is concentrated. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds, (2) the spectral energy values across frequency bins within the band, (3) the energy threshold percentage (default 85%). Computed by sorting frequency bins in ascending order by frequency and accumulating energy until the accumulated energy reaches the threshold fraction of the band's total energy; the frequency at that point is the rolloff point. Indicates the spectral 'brightness' or high-frequency content within a band. Displayed as a scalar time series over analysis frames. [formal: reiectura spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Breathy voice (breathy phonation) is a classification category for a mode of voiced phonation defined by a specific glottal configuration: the vocal folds vibrate periodically at a normal fundamental frequency, but the glottis does not fully close during each cycle, so turbulent air leaks through the residual gap and adds noise to the harmonic signal, producing an audible breathy or airy timbre. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal configuration — incomplete medial closure during the vibration cycle, (2) the cycle signature — modal f0 with a shortened closed phase (a low closure quotient) and a turbulent noise leak, (3) the acoustic signature — a breathy timbre with reduced harmonic-to-noise contrast. It persists as a named mode of the phonation-mode taxonomy: documented in laryngology and phonetics, used in voice-disorder assessment (breathy voice in vocal fold paresis, as a habitual voice quality, or after laryngeal surgery) and in voice training (breathy quality contrasted with modal voice), and maintained alongside the other voice modes. e.g.: the breathy voice quality labeled in a voice-disorder assessment of a teacher with a vocal fold nodule; the breathy category in Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory; the breathy voice quality labeled in a laryngology report for a patient with left vocal fold paresis | not: creaky voice (low-frequency aperiodic implosive vibration, a different mode); whisper voice (unvoiced glottal airflow, outside voiced phonation); modal phonation (complete glottal closure each cycle, a different mode) [formal: vox aspera | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

Computational linguistics is a disciplinary framework for formalizing linguistic knowledge in algorithms and computational models. Parameters: corpus design, statistical models, symbolic grammars, evaluation metrics, processing pipelines. It persists via open-source software, benchmark datasets, peer-reviewed publications, and university curricula that replicate model performance across tasks.

A temporal-feature is a numerical descriptor extracted from the time-domain representation (waveform, energy envelope, or amplitude modulation) of an audio signal that captures a measurable aspect of its temporal structure. The n-th moment of the energy envelope, the rate of sign changes in the signal, and the time to reach peak energy are canonical instances. Parameters: (1) the temporal domain source — the discrete-time waveform, the short-time energy envelope, or the amplitude modulation envelope from which the feature is computed; (2) the computation — the specific mathematical operation applied (e.g., weighted mean of time indices for centroid, count of sign transitions for zero-crossing rate, first threshold-crossing time for attack); (3) dimensionality — whether the result is a single scalar, a time series, or a binary flag. Persistence mechanism: standardized mathematical definitions used across audio analysis, music information retrieval, and speech processing toolkits (librosa, Essentia, HTK, Praat) and encoded in published feature extraction pipelines. [formal: characteristicum temporale | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The ratio of the maximum magnitude bin in a spectrum to the root-mean-square magnitude across all bins. Parameters: (1) discrete magnitude spectrum |X[k]| for k = 0, …, N−1, where N is the number of frequency bins, (2) the index k_max at which |X[k]| is maximized. Persistence mechanism: computed as C_spectral = |X[k_max]| / sqrt((1/N) * Σ|X[k]|²), where the sum spans all bins. The ratio is a dimensionless scalar. Display trailer: spectral-crest-factor is a dimensionless quantity, typically expressed in decibels as 20·log₁₀(C_spectral). [formal: cresta spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Dysphonia is a human-made clinical diagnostic category that groups presentations of voice disorder by their underlying laryngeal mechanism: organic (structural or inflammatory causes such as nodules, polyps, or paresis), functional (behavioral causes such as muscle-tension phonation), and neurogenic (neurological causes such as spasmodic or palsy-driven presentations). Its members are the diagnostic presentations the discipline recognizes and reports — hoarse, breathy, strained, or weak voice attributed to a named mechanism — not the individual lesions or signal parameters themselves. Parameters: (1) the mechanism class that assigns a presentation to the category (organic, functional, neurogenic), (2) the presentation the clinician reports (voice quality, pitch range, phonation effort), (3) the coding and reference conventions the discipline maintains (ICD-10-CM R49.0, exclusion of non-laryngeal causes). Persistence: maintained by the disciplines of laryngology and speech-language pathology — standardized in ICD-10-CM coding, recorded in clinical guidelines and consultation reports, taught in clinical curricula, and revised as diagnostic standards evolve. e.g.: the ICD-10-CM code R49.0 (Dysphonia) assigned in a hospital discharge record; an organic dysphonia due to vocal fold nodules diagnosis in a laryngology consultation report; a spasmodic dysphonia classification in a speech-language pathology evaluation report | not: a vocal fold nodule (a lesion that can cause a presentation the category groups, not itself a presentation); jitter (a voice-quality parameter measured from the signal, not a diagnostic category); dysphagia (a swallowing disorder, a different clinical territory) [formal: affectio vocis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

The spectral kurtosis is the kurtosis (fourth standardized moment) of the spectral power distribution across frequency bins. Parameters: (1) the power-spectrum over which kurtosis is computed, (2) the normalization reference (typically the mean power squared). Computation: kurtosis = E[(P - μ)^4] / E[(P - μ)^2]^2 where P is the power spectrum and μ is its mean. The measure detects impulsive or non-stationary components in a signal by identifying frequency bins with heavy-tailed power distributions. The construct persists as a single scalar value per analyzed segment. Display: scalar, typically expressed in decibels. [formal: kurtosis spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A processing technique in which a signal's amplitude envelope is extracted and used to modulate or track another signal. Parameters: (1) input signal x(t), (2) envelope extraction stage (rectification followed by low-pass filtering with time constant τ, or Hilbert transform followed by magnitude extraction), (3) output modulation rate governed by attack time τ_a and decay/release time τ_r. Persistence mechanism: the envelope e(t) is computed as e(t) = LP{x(t) · h_LP(t)} where h_LP is a low-pass filter impulse response characterized by τ_a for upward transitions and τ_r for downward transitions; this envelope then drives a gain stage, frequency shifter, or other parameterized element. Display trailer: envelope-following is a behavioral pattern instantiated in specific circuits or algorithms such as auto-wah, tremolo, or sidechain compression. [formal: sequentia involucri | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Delta coefficients are first-order time derivatives of cepstral coefficients, capturing the temporal trajectory of the spectral envelope. Computed by fitting a least-squares linear regression over a window of cepstral coefficient frames. Used in speech recognition to model temporal dynamics beyond static spectral shape. [formal: coefficients delta | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Linguistic register is the map of the system of situationally differentiated language varieties a speech community develops and maintains — the varieties a community deploys for different communicative situations (colloquial, formal, technical, ceremonial, professional) — carved along three parameters. (1) The situational axis: the dimensions along which the varieties are organized are field (the subject matter and activity in which the language is deployed), tenor (the social relations and roles between participants), and mode (the channel and the participatory structure of the discourse); a variety is a conventionalized set of lexical, grammatical, and prosodic choices indexed to the situation, so that the same speaker deploys different varieties in different situations. (2) The boundary lines that separate the map from its neighbours: register is indexed to situation, which distinguishes it from dialect (indexed to region and social group) and from genre (a type of discourse text rather than a variety of the language itself); and it is distinct from the institutional register — an official list maintained by an authority with legal or institutional force — in that a linguistic register is updated by the speech community's convention, not by institutional mandate, and no authority stands behind its entries. (3) The map, not the territory: the entry names the systematic description the community and the discipline build over the natural variation of speech — the inventory of varieties and the dimensions that organize it — not the natural variation itself. Persistence: the varieties persist as social convention — acquired in socialization, maintained through institutional reinforcement (courts, academies, professions, liturgy), and relearned by each generation; the map persists as the stable sub-field of linguistics called register analysis, its dimensions codified in textbooks and corpora. [formal: regiter linguae | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

Voice break is a human-made clinical event in phonation: the abrupt, involuntary interruption or discontinuity in the voice signal during sustained phonation or pitch gliding, caused by laryngeal muscle fatigue or dysfunction. It is observed as a sudden drop in intensity, a sudden shift to falsetto, or a complete cessation of phonation at a particular pitch or loudness level. It persists as a recognized clinical sign because it is defined by an observable auditory and acoustic event during voice assessment. e.g.: a voice break heard during a sustained vowel phonation in a patient with vocal fold paresis; a voice break observed during a pitch glide in a voice disorder assessment; a voice break documented in a clinical voice evaluation report | not: jitter (cycle-to-cycle frequency variation, not an interruption of phonation); phonation arrest (complete cessation of phonation due to vocal fold adduction failure, not a momentary break) [formal: vocis interruptus | substrate: behavior | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

Neurolinguistics is a human-made interdisciplinary field — the study of the neural and biological mechanisms that underlie language acquisition, processing, representation, and comprehension. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the explanatory level is biological/neural (brain anatomy, neural circuits, electrophysiological responses, neuroimaging data, lesion studies, and molecular markers), not purely behavioral or computational; (2) the phenomenon explained is language in its full range — phonology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, lexicon, acquisition, and breakdown — treated as operations implemented by neural systems. Neurolinguistics persists as an active research enterprise that generates testable hypotheses about how the brain implements language, uses these hypotheses to interpret clinical conditions (aphasia, dyslexia, speech disorders), and informs brain-computer interfaces for language restoration. Paradigmatic methods: fMRI and EEG mapping of language tasks, lesion-symptom mapping in aphasia patients, intracranial electrophysiology, and computational modeling of neural language processing. [formal: neurolinguistica | substrate: brain | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Spectral-smoothness is a spectral analysis measure that quantifies how smoothly the per-bin energy values change across frequency in a full spectrum. It computes a weighted mean absolute derivative of adjacent bin energies, normalized by the spectrum's mean energy and the total number of bins, yielding a dimensionless index of spectral continuity. Parameters: (1) the spectral estimate (periodogram, Welch's method, or spectrogram slice), (2) the per-bin energy vector across all frequency bins. Computed as smoothness = 1 - (1/N) * Σ|E[i+1] - E[i]| / mean(E) where E[i] is the energy of bin i, N is the number of bins, and mean(E) is the arithmetic mean of all bin energies. Values range from 0 (highly irregular spectrum with abrupt energy changes) to approaching 1 (very smooth spectrum with gradual energy transitions). Displayed as a scalar time series over analysis frames. [formal: planities spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.30]

The glottogram (glottal-flow waveform) is a human-made time-series representation of estimated glottal airflow obtained by inverse filtering the speech signal. The speech signal x(n) is processed with the inverse of the estimated vocal-tract transfer function — the inverse linear-prediction filter 1/(1 - Σ_k a_k z^-k) over voiced frames — yielding the glottal-flow sequence g(n). Parameters: (1) the speech signal x(n) frame-aligned to voicing, (2) the vocal-tract filter estimate as linear-prediction coefficients a_k with prediction order p, (3) the frame and windowing parameters of the inverse filter. The glottogram encodes the excitation of the source-filter model: its derivatives (contact quotient, open quotient, return phase, asymmetry coefficient) constitute the voice-quality measurement family. Persistence mechanism: implemented in speech analysis toolkits (Praat, MATLAB, Kaldi), documented in speech science textbooks, and used clinically to estimate glottal flow for voice-disorder analysis; persists as per-frame estimated flow values and their derived parameters. [formal: glottalis fluxus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Intonation is the constructed linguistic framework for analyzing pitch-contour organization in spoken language: the way fundamental frequency rises and falls across the duration of an utterance, and the way those movements are patterned by linguistic rule rather than speaker whim. Parameters: (1) pitch contour - the F0 trajectory across the utterance, rising, falling, or level; (2) tone unit - the stretch of speech over which a single contour operates, delimited by pauses; (3) nuclear stress - the syllable carrying the principal tone of the tone unit; (4) grammatical and attitudinal function - contour used to mark clause type (interrogative vs declarative), focus, and attitude (e.g., English rising terminals for yes-no questions). Persistence: intonation is realized in every produced utterance, analyzed in intonation notation (e.g., ToBI), taught in language pedagogy, and studied in phonology; it persists as long as speech carries meaning through pitch. [formal: intonatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The crest factor of a signal is the ratio of its peak amplitude to its root-mean-square value. Parameters: (1) the signal samples x[n] over an analysis window, (2) the peak amplitude max|x[n]|, (3) the RMS value computed over the same window. Computation: crest = max|x[n]| / RMS(x[n]). Display: [DSP: descriptor, units: dimensionless]

It persists via published reconstructions, philological editions, comparative datasets, and university curricula that transmit methodological standards across generations.

The source-filter model is a human-made mathematical model of speech production that decomposes the speech signal generation into a source component, typically the glottal airflow with fundamental frequency, and a filter component, the vocal tract transfer function shaping formants. Parameters: source excitation model, filter order, formant frequencies and bandwidths, glottal pulse shape. Persistence mechanism: the model is formalized in equations, implemented in speech synthesis and analysis software, and taught in speech science curricula; it persists as a reusable theoretical framework. [formal: source-filter-model | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.07]

Spectral-band-energy is a spectral analysis parameter representing the total energy accumulated within a defined frequency sub-band of a spectrum at a given analysis frame. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds (e.g., ISO 266 third-octave band edges or arbitrary analyst-specified limits), (2) the spectral resolution (frequency bin width) of the underlying transform. Computed as the sum of squared magnitude values |X[k]|² across all frequency bins k whose center frequencies fall within [f_low, f_high). The result is a scalar energy value per frame, typically expressed in joules or a normalized relative scale. Maximum phonation time (MPT) is the voice-quality parameter measuring the longest duration a person can sustain a comfortable phonation, reported in seconds: the patient takes a deep breath and phonates a comfortable-pitch /a/ (or a comfortable syllable such as /pa/) for as long as possible, and the examiner times the total voiced duration with a stopwatch from voice onset to voice offset, including any breaks in the phonation. Its parameters are: (1) the task and prompt — a single maximal breath, comfortable pitch, sustained /a/ or /pa/, (2) the timing method — total wall-clock duration of the phonation, including pauses, (3) the reference range maintained by the discipline — about 15-17 s in healthy adults, with shorter times flagging either vocal-fold pathology or reduced respiratory support, and re-measurements that isolate the two. It is reported in seconds and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in laryngology suites and voice-screening checklists, taught in speech-language pathology curricula, and maintained alongside the GRBAS scale, jitter, shimmer, and the perturbation and phase quotients. e.g.: the MPT recorded as 8.4 s for a laryngectomized patient in a laryngology clinic intake; the MPT value of 12.1 s in a voice-disorder screening report for a teacher with vocal fatigue; the MPT baseline of 16.5 s maintained in a pre-treatment voice-assessment battery for a singer with vocal nodules | not: glottal-flow waveform duration (a per-cycle quantity); jitter (period perturbation, a relative measure); subglottal pressure (a transducer-measured pressure, not a timed duration) [formal: tempus phonationis maximum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

Harmonicity is a human-made audio analysis feature that quantifies how closely a signal's spectral content matches a periodic (harmonic) model versus a noise-like model. It is computed by comparing the energy of spectral peaks that align with a harmonic template (partials at integer multiples of a fundamental frequency f0) to the residual energy that falls between those partials. Parameters: (1) a fundamental frequency estimate f0, (2) the number of harmonic partials to consider, (3) a tolerance window around each partial bin, (4) the power spectrum from which energy is measured. The persistence mechanism is the ratio H = E_harmonic / (E_harmonic + E_residual), yielding a value in [0, 1], where 1 indicates perfect harmonicity and 0 indicates pure noise. Cognitive-linguistics is a human-made approach to linguistics — the study of language as a manifestation of general cognitive abilities, including categorization, conceptualization, metaphorical reasoning, and embodied experience. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the explanatory framework denies that language operates as an autonomous module separate from general cognition; language structure reflects domain-general cognitive mechanisms like attention, memory, pattern recognition, and conceptual blending; (2) the empirical evidence comes from cross-linguistic analysis of how semantic structure, syntactic patterns, and figurative language systematically reflect cognitive universals (spatial reasoning, embodiment, force-dynamics) rather than language-internal formal rules. Cognitive-linguistics persists as a theoretical framework that produces models of construction grammar, conceptual metaphor theory, and cognitive semantics, generating testable predictions about language use, acquisition, and processing that compete with modularist accounts. Paradigmatic cases: conceptual metaphor analysis (e.g., ARGUMENT IS WAR), construction grammar descriptions, image-schema theory. The area-velocity model is a speech-science computational construct that estimates the glottal cross-sectional area waveform A(t) from the inverse-filtered glottal-flow signal g(n) using a first-order differential relationship between area and flow velocity. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and a local flow velocity estimate v, the model computes A(t) = g(n) / v(t), where v is the characteristic velocity of airflow through the glottal aperture, parameterized by the estimated glottal area at a reference point (typically the open quotient peak) and the assumed flow regime (incompressible, quasi-steady). Its parameters are: (1) the glottal-flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, the primary operand, (2) the local flow velocity v(t) - a parameterized estimate of airflow velocity through the glottis, (3) the reference area A_ref - the glottal area at a known point (e.g., maximum opening), used to calibrate the velocity parameter, (4) the flow-regime assumption - incompressible, quasi-steady flow, (5) the reconstruction route - direct division or iterative optimization over the pitch-synchronous cycle. A well-calibrated area-velocity model yields a physically consistent A(t) waveform suitable for deriving the area-quotient family (open, closed, contact quotients). It is reported as the estimated area waveform per cycle and persists as a standard inference method in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in the glottal area-velocity literature (e.g., the Shujman model, Alku area-velocity method), and maintained as part of the glottal source analysis pipeline. e.g.: the Shujman area-velocity model implemented in the Praat AreaVel plugin; the Alku area-velocity method as described in Alku et al. 1996 Journal of the Acoustical Society of America; the area-velocity reconstruction in the VoiceSaw glottal source analysis toolkit | not: glottal flow g(n) (the raw waveform the model takes as input, not the area estimate); inverse filtering (the preprocessing step before the area-velocity model receives its input) [formal: modelus areae velocitatis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

The glottal cycle is the periodic open/close cycle of the glottis during voiced phonation, comprising the opening phase (glottal opening from closed to open), the closed phase (vocal folds in contact), and the transition phases (closing and opening). It is measured per pitch period from the glottal-flow waveform or the electroglottogram envelope. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0, the glottal cycle is partitioned into phases: opening (from the flow maximum to the minimum), closed (the flow at or near zero), and closing (from the minimum back to the maximum). Its parameters include the open quotient (ratio of open-phase duration to the period), the contact quotient (from the electroglottogram envelope), the asymmetry coefficient (ratio of open-phase to close-phase duration), and the return phase (time from flow maximum to return to baseline). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software from the glottogram and electroglottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. [formal: cyclus glottis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Cepstral-mean-variance normalization (CMVN) is a signal processing technique that normalizes cepstral coefficient vectors by computing the mean and variance across an utterance (or a sliding window) and applying z-score normalization to each frame. Parameters: (1) the mean is computed per coefficient dimension across all frames, (2) the variance is computed per coefficient dimension across all frames, (3) the normalization is applied element-wise as (c_i - μ_i) / σ_i for each coefficient c_i, where σ_i is the standard deviation. The technique removes both channel-induced mean shifts and variance mismatches between speakers. Persistence mechanism: implemented as a standard preprocessing step in speech recognition pipelines (Kaldi, HTK) and encoded in audio processing libraries (Python, MATLAB). The phonation threshold pressure (PTP) is a laryngeal voice-quality parameter quantifying the minimum subglottal pressure at which vocal-fold vibration begins. It is measured by ramping the subglottal pressure (or driving flow) upward through a pressure transducer — a catheter below the glottis in vivo, or a pressure line in an excised-laryx or in-vitro laryx rig — and reading the pressure value at the onset of sustained vocal-fold oscillation, reported in cmH2O or kPa. A high PTP indicates increased vocal-fold load or stiffness (hyperfunctional phonation, edema, paresis with compensatory effort); a low PTP indicates low fold tension or hypofunction. Its parameters are: (1) the measurement setup — in-vivo catheter, excised-laryx rig, or in-vitro laryx model; (2) the pressure ramp rate and the threshold criterion (first sustained oscillation of the glottal flow or fold vibration); (3) the vocal-fold state (tension, adduction, mass) the ramp is applied to; (4) the pressure reference and reporting unit. It is distinct from the subglottal pressure SGP, which is the steady-state or cycle-averaged pressure measured during ongoing phonation, while PTP is the threshold at the onset of phonation. It persists as a standardized clinical and experimental parameter documented in laryngology and voice-surgery literature, and maintained as a member of the voice-quality measurement map. e.g.: phonation threshold pressure measured by a pressure ramp in an excised-laryx study of vocal-fold stiffness; phonation threshold pressure reported in a cadaveric larynx biomechanics study comparing fold tension levels; phonation threshold pressure recorded in an in-vivo laryngeal-effort assessment using a nasotracheal catheter | not: subglottal pressure SGP (the steady-state pressure during ongoing phonation, not the onset threshold); glottal flow waveform g(t) (the output of phonation, not its onset pressure); sound-pressure level at the glottis [formal: limen pressio subglottalis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

A transfer function is the representation of a linear time-invariant system as the ratio of the transform of its output to the transform of its input with zero initial conditions: H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) in the Laplace domain for continuous-time systems, H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) in the Z domain for discrete-time systems. Parameters: (1) the LTI system whose input-output relation is mapped, (2) the complex domain of the representation (s or z), (3) the numerator and denominator polynomials, whose roots place the system's zeros and poles. The function persists through mathematical notation in control and signal-processing textbooks, engineering standards, and reproducible implementations; engineers use it to analyze stability, predict frequency response, and design controllers and filters. [formal: functio transferens | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Derivation is a human-made morphological operation — the process by which a language creates a new lexeme from an existing one by adding derivational material. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) lexeme change: the output is a new lexeme with a distinct dictionary identity from the input (happy → happiness is one lexeme becoming another; walk → walked is NOT derivation, because walked is an inflected form of the same lexeme as walk). This lexeme-change criterion is the decisive boundary from inflection. (2) derivational material: the operation is carried by a bound morpheme (affix) or, in some languages, by a change of stress, vowel, or other internal modification that contributes derivational meaning (English sing → song: an ablaut-derived noun; by contrast the tense forms sang and sung remain inflected forms of the same lexeme as sing). (3) conventionalized meaning: the derivational material contributes a systematic, predictable meaning (-ness 'state of being', un- 'negation', -er 'agent') that transforms the input lexeme's meaning in a rule-governed way. Paradigmatic cases: happy + -ness → happiness (new lexeme); write → writer (new lexeme, agentive). Derivation persists as a productive rule — speakers coin new derived lexemes on the fly — and as a stable category of grammatical description: derivational affixes are catalogued in the morphological inventory of each language. [formal: derivatio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]
